<reason>Side B kept the easier comparative: messy public bands and rates still beat a locked drawer, and the motion already prices in lost flexibility. CON’s implementation attacks (wide ranges, manager-written captions, redaction, Goodhart) were sharp, but B answered them as design limits rather than a veto, and A never really engaged that even a wide range still has a floor and a tell. A’s dual-audience reply (noise to workers, leash on managers) was the cleverest move, yet it left B’s core claim standing: if the numbers constrain pay, workers have a check they did not have before, and an outside offer prices an exit rather than the job already held.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s trap that CON cannot treat the numbers as both too noisy to inform and sharp enough to compress pay or kill roles, crystallized as “if managers feel a leash, workers have seen a price.”</best_rebuttal>
